description_ru: Юмористический рассказ о сборке шкафа по бессловесной инструкции и о тщетности человеческого оптимизма.
text:
The box arrived on a Tuesday, and I should have known from its weight that it contained not furniture but a philosophical challenge. It was the size of a coffin and covered in pictograms of a small, faceless man who appeared, in every frame, to be either assembling a wardrobe or being slowly consumed by one. The wardrobe was called Skrömbel, which in Swedish presumably means "a gentle lie."

I opened it with the confidence that has been the downfall of all great civilisations. Inside lay one hundred and forty-seven components, nested like a dismal Russian doll, together with a small bag of screws, a minuscule Allen key and an instruction leaflet, which, in the interests of international harmony, contained no words whatever. Page one showed two people smiling at the finished wardrobe. This struck me as optimistic. Page two showed the same smiling people, with a suspicious absence of sweat, holding a hammer.

For the first hour, I made excellent progress, in the sense that a man in a rowing boat makes excellent progress before he realises it is tied to the dock. I identified the panels, sorted the screws into small heaps, and fastened Panel B to Panel F, only to discover that Panel F was in fact Panel P, a near-twin whose only distinguishing feature was a hole on the side that, in retrospect, I should have regarded as a warning.

By the second hour, a creeping sense of grievance had set in. The small faceless man, I noticed, seemed to possess three hands. Step nine required me to insert dowel A into hole 12, a manoeuvre that, by my calculation, would only be possible if the wardrobe were rotated through a fourth dimension. I rang my brother-in-law, a structural engineer, who listened in silence for ninety seconds and then said, with the weary gentleness of a doctor delivering news, "Put down the hammer, Daniel."

I did not put down the hammer. Instead, as the light failed, I entered what I can only describe as a trance. I no longer saw a wardrobe. I saw an adversary. I spoke to it. I called it names that a Swedish carpenter would blush to learn. At one point, I believe I threatened to burn it, and the wardrobe, with typical Scandinavian equanimity, simply leaned a little to the left.

At ten past midnight, I stepped back. There it stood: a tall, rather handsome object, of whose structural integrity I had no doubt whatsoever, apart from the leftover bag containing fourteen screws, six brackets and a mysterious wooden peg. I regard the surplus as a sort of dividend. Any piece of furniture that survives with fewer parts than were supplied, I reason, is proof of an efficient design.

I opened the door, and admired the bare interior. The door, after a thoughtful pause, fell off. This was followed, in a suitably dramatic sequence, by a shelf, a side panel and a small noise that I choose to interpret as applause.

I now live with Skrömbel in a state of cautious, mutual respect. The door is attached with tape, which I have convinced myself is a design feature, in the tradition of the great Japanese art of repairing pottery with gold. My shirts hang within, at a tilt of precisely seven degrees, and I find that I walk past it with a faint feeling of reverence, as one might pass an elderly relative who has been through a great deal, and has not forgiven me.

My advice to anyone considering such a purchase is brief. Buy the boxed set. Hire a professional. Or, at the very least, learn to read hieroglyphics, since it is evident that the faceless man did not.

focus_sounds.tip_ru: Губы округлены и вытянуты, зубов не касаются: wardrobe — не «вордроб».
Рот открыт шире, чем для «э»: звук между «а» и «э».
p, t, k в начале ударного слога — с лёгким выдохом.
На конце слова b, d, g остаются звонкими: не «Скрёмбел» с глухим «п».
